forces.title: Hardware commoditization drives medtech shift to software
forces.description: The medtech industry is undergoing a structural shift where hardware categories are maturing and facing increasing price pressure. This compels companies to increasingly rely on software as a critical avenue for differentiation, growth, and patient impact, pushing them towards new business models and value propositions.
forces.source_title: The future of delivering software as a medical device

forces.title: Software enabling new recurring revenue models for medtech
forces.description: Software is creating significant upside for medtech by enabling new recurring revenue models. This includes premium analytics layers and subscription-based services, moving away from traditional capital sales. This shift increases customer stickiness and allows companies to generate consistent income streams beyond initial device purchases, improving financial predictability and valuation.
forces.source_title: The future of delivering software as a medical device

forces.title: AI advances rapidly improve software productivity for medtech
forces.description: Advances in AI are significantly boosting software productivity across industries, including medtech, with organizations seeing 30% to 70% gains in development efficiency. This represents a structural change, creating both an opportunity and an imperative for medtech companies to harness these gains while upholding stringent quality, safety, and regulatory compliance standards, accelerating innovation cycles.
forces.source_title: The future of delivering software as a medical device

forces.title: Traditional regulatory processes hinder medtech software development speed
forces.description: Medtech software development remains hampered by phased, documentation-heavy regulatory and quality standards, unlike agile models in other industries. These processes extend timelines by 20% to 30%, inflate development costs, and erode business cases, creating a significant impediment to rapid innovation and market responsiveness for regulated software, including SaMD.
forces.source_title: The future of delivering software as a medical device

forces.title: Rising cybersecurity threats challenge medtech software quality and trust
forces.description: Cybersecurity is an increasingly vital aspect of medtech software quality, with expanding connected devices, digital ecosystems, and AI-enabled capabilities creating new attack vectors. Medtech organizations face pressure to integrate cybersecurity throughout the development life cycle to meet evolving regulatory expectations and protect patient safety, as AI-driven vulnerability discovery compresses exploitation times, posing significant risks.
forces.source_title: The future of delivering software as a medical device

forces.title: Integrating SaMD with hardware creates significant development challenges
forces.description: While software as a medical device (SaMD) enables faster innovation, its integration with hardware presents a major challenge for medtech organizations. Product development timelines and frameworks for software and hardware differ substantially, complicating the synchronization required for integrated solutions. This divergence creates a capability gap in delivering SaMD at speed while maintaining regulatory quality and successful hardware integration.
forces.source_title: The future of delivering software as a medical device

forces.title: Modernizing software development attracts talent and reduces burden
forces.description: Modernizing software development functions is crucial for medtech to attract and retain digital talent and improve efficiency. By enhancing engineering practices, reducing regulatory burden through process design and automation, and adopting more efficient workflows, organizations can create environments where engineers focus on high-value activities. This strategic shift improves the industry's ability to compete for essential skills needed for future growth.
forces.source_title: The future of delivering software as a medical device

forces.title: European HTA frameworks raise evidence bar for novel devices
forces.description: Evolving Health Technology Assessment (HTA) frameworks in the EU are increasing the evidence requirements for medical devices. These systems increasingly demand formal 'comparative effectiveness' data, proving a new device's superiority over existing treatments. Many existing clinical programs, particularly those from Asia-Pacific challengers, are not equipped to provide this, creating a significant barrier to market entry and adoption in European markets.
forces.source_title: Building Global Champions: The Asia-Pacific Region’s Next Medtech Wave

forces.title: Inadequate IP protection restricts global medtech expansion
forces.description: Delayed global intellectual property (IP) filings by emerging medtech companies severely limit their strategic options for international expansion, licensing, partnerships, or acquisitions. Global buyers conduct rigorous due diligence, and gaps in patent coverage in key markets like the EU can significantly compress valuations or narrow exit opportunities, making early and robust IP strategy critical for long-term success.
forces.source_title: Building Global Champions: The Asia-Pacific Region’s Next Medtech Wave

forces.title: Robust Quality Management Systems crucial for export success
forces.description: Investing in an exportable Quality Management System (QMS) and comprehensive documentation before scaling production is critical for medtech companies. This proactive approach helps avoid the high costs and delays associated with retrofitting systems later, ensuring compliance with international standards (e.g., ISO 13485) and facilitating smoother market entry and regulatory approvals in regions like the EU.
forces.source_title: Building Global Champions: The Asia-Pacific Region’s Next Medtech Wave

forces.title: Staff shortages boost demand for remote care technologies
forces.description: Severe staff shortages across European healthcare, exacerbated by an aging workforce and heavy workloads, are intensifying the demand for innovative solutions. This trend makes remote care technology, including medical devices and wearables for remote monitoring, an absolute necessity. It serves as a critical solution to ease pressure on hospitals, enhance capacity, and maintain care quality amidst growing demand.
forces.source_title: How technology could cut millions of hospital visits across Europe

forces.title: High upfront costs impede widespread remote monitoring adoption
forces.description: The adoption of remote monitoring technologies faces a significant barrier due to high upfront spending. This includes investments in IT adjustments, digital platforms, and potentially new monitoring/measurement equipment. Furthermore, costs associated with changing workflows and staff training or recruitment add to the financial burden, particularly for European hospitals with limited profit margins, hindering scale-up.
forces.source_title: How technology could cut millions of hospital visits across Europe

forces.title: Fragmented reimbursement slows remote monitoring scale-up in EU
forces.description: Fragmented and often incomplete reimbursement policies for remote monitoring across Europe hinder its widespread adoption. Providers operate under different budgets and healthcare laws, creating perverse incentives and complicating cooperation. Insufficient coverage of all costs, especially during the high-cost start-up phase per patient, acts as a significant brake, preventing the necessary financial support for large-scale implementation.
forces.source_title: How technology could cut millions of hospital visits across Europe

forces.title: Poor data exchange infrastructure impedes remote care scaling
forces.description: Effective scaling of remote monitoring is hindered by inadequate data exchange between IT systems, applications, and healthcare providers in many EU countries. Smooth, uniform recording and sharing of patient data are crucial for coordinated care and correct interpretation of monitoring data. Countries like Ireland and the Netherlands still need significant improvement to achieve the necessary interoperability and complete patient view.
forces.source_title: How technology could cut millions of hospital visits across Europe

forces.title: Medtech's M&A-driven complexity necessitates shared services
forces.description: Decades of acquisition-led growth in medtech have created significant operational debt, leading to fragmented ERP systems, inconsistent processes, and decentralized structures. This compounding complexity, alongside continued M&A as a strategic imperative, highlights the need for enterprise shared services. These services simplify operations, enable faster integration of acquired businesses, and create a scalable operating model to absorb future growth.
forces.source_title: Enterprise Shared Services in Medtech: The Only Wrong Move Is Standing Still

forces.title: Contracting gross margins pressure medtech to cut G&A costs
forces.description: Gross margins for the largest public medtech companies have contracted by 149 basis points since 2019, intensifying pressure to expand operating income. With continuous cuts to R&D and commercial execution risking growth, general and administrative (G&A) expenses become the primary target for cost reduction. This financial pressure drives the imperative for solutions like enterprise shared services to streamline back-office operations.
forces.source_title: Enterprise Shared Services in Medtech: The Only Wrong Move Is Standing Still

forces.title: AI adoption stalled by lack of process and data foundations
forces.description: Despite AI being an executive mandate, its scaling into full production within medtech is significantly limited by the absence of foundational process and data infrastructure. Standardized workflows, consolidated data, and concentrated volume are essential for AI to perform accurately and efficiently. Without these, AI initiatives often stall, preventing companies from realizing the technology's full potential for productivity and performance improvement.
forces.source_title: Enterprise Shared Services in Medtech: The Only Wrong Move Is Standing Still

forces.title: Customer expectations reshape medtech service delivery via 'Amazon effect'
forces.description: The 'Amazon effect' has fundamentally reshaped customer expectations in medtech, with buyers demanding greater visibility and seamless experiences comparable to consumer e-commerce. Fragmented customer interactions, such as multiple bills from the same parent company for different brands, reveal operational debt and create competitive vulnerability. This shift drives medtech to build customer-centric solutions and operations into shared services to improve loyalty and satisfaction.
forces.source_title: Enterprise Shared Services in Medtech: The Only Wrong Move Is Standing Still

forces.title: Expanded shared services scope unlocks new medtech efficiencies
forces.description: Leading medtech companies are extending the scope of enterprise shared services beyond traditional G&A functions to include knowledge-based, high-value areas. This expansion covers clinical and regulatory activities (e.g., trial design, submissions), quality (e.g., CAPA, supplier audits), and R&D (e.g., prototype development). This trend, amplified by AI tools, offers significant productivity gains, cost reductions, and improved performance in specialized functions.
forces.source_title: Enterprise Shared Services in Medtech: The Only Wrong Move Is Standing Still

forces.title: Human resistance to change hinders AI adoption in life sciences
forces.description: The primary reason AI efforts in life sciences often stall is human unwillingness to adapt work processes, rather than technological limitations. Scaling AI requires role modeling from senior leaders, targeted training, consistent reinforcement, and rewiring incentives to encourage adoption. Without addressing this human factor, even perfect data infrastructure and technology will fail to deliver impact, leading to a lack of transformation.
forces.source_title: AI in life sciences explained: The technology that could reinvent medicine

forces.title: Maintaining trust and compliance critical for AI in medtech
forces.description: For AI in medtech, building and maintaining trust and compliance is paramount; losing them jeopardizes competitive edge and patient safety. AI outputs must be explainable, interpretable ('glass box'), and supported by clear validation, auditability, and documentation of AI-informed decisions. Despite life sciences' strong culture of data reliability, rigorous testing, validation, and guardrails against risks like 'hallucination' must remain high.
forces.source_title: AI in life sciences explained: The technology that could reinvent medicine

viewpoints.title: Early SaMD innovation essential for future medtech leadership
viewpoints.description: McKinsey believes that medtech organizations prioritizing high-quality software, delivered with speed, will define the next generation of innovation. Successfully integrating software as a medical device (SaMD) with hardware, while maintaining regulatory-grade quality, is identified as the sector's defining capability gap. Organizations that move early to address this challenge by transforming their operating models for rapid and high-quality SaMD delivery will be best positioned to lead.
viewpoints.source_title: The future of delivering software as a medical device

viewpoints.title: Delaying shared services strategy in medtech risks competitive lag
viewpoints.description: Bain argues that the only wrong move for medtech companies regarding enterprise shared services is not having a clear strategy or delaying its implementation. As competitors streamline processes, build shared capabilities, and integrate AI into workflows, companies that wait risk falling behind significantly in performance, valuation, and talent attraction, highlighting the urgency for strategic action in this area.
viewpoints.source_title: Enterprise Shared Services in Medtech: The Only Wrong Move Is Standing Still

viewpoints.title: AI is a transformative, holistic force for life sciences, including medtech
viewpoints.description: McKinsey asserts that AI is a uniquely broad, fast, and holistic technological cycle transforming life sciences, including medtech, unlike any previous wave. It enables unprecedented access to human knowledge, faster experimentation, and the breakdown of organizational silos. AI's potential extends beyond R&D to transform how the entire enterprise operates, offering significant value capture opportunities across scientific and operational workflows.
viewpoints.source_title: AI in life sciences explained: The technology that could reinvent medicine

viewpoints.title: Remote care technology is becoming critical for European hospitals
viewpoints.description: ING Think views remote care technology as an absolute necessity for European hospitals. Faced with severe staff shortages, an aging workforce, and rising demand from aging populations and chronic conditions, remote monitoring offers a unique solution. It can reduce avoidable visits, improve care quality, and increase capacity, making its adoption a critical response to mounting pressures in the healthcare sector.
viewpoints.source_title: How technology could cut millions of hospital visits across Europe

viewpoints.title: Medtech industry faces talent gap for digital and tech skills
viewpoints.description: McKinsey highlights that the medtech industry struggles to attract and retain digital, technology, and analytics talent compared to adjacent industries. Medtech organizations are often perceived as less attractive due to a lower employee value proposition and limited availability of key technical skills, particularly in application development. This talent gap poses a significant challenge for future growth and innovation in the sector.
viewpoints.source_title: The future of delivering software as a medical device

viewpoints.title: Pharmaceuticals and medical articles retail show strong resilience
viewpoints.description: Allianz_ie reports that the retail subsectors of 'Pharmaceuticals, Medical & Cosmetic Articles' are demonstrating stronger performance amidst a challenging trading environment in Ireland. While overall retail sales volumes are declining, these categories are experiencing positive growth. This resilience suggests robust underlying demand or a less discretionary nature of these products, allowing them to counter broader consumer spending pressures.

demand_drivers.driver: Ageing populations and rising chronic conditions
demand_drivers.description: Increase demand for continuous care and monitoring, which remote patient monitoring can efficiently address.
Remote care frees up capacity and reduces the burden on overstretched medical personnel, making technology a critical solution.

new_opportunities.description: Large opportunity to provide devices and services to reduce hospital admissions by 6.5 million and consultations by 23 million annually across the EU.

market_sizing.methodology: Analysis based on expert interviews and 35 scientific studies, estimating 50% of hospital care suitable for remote patient monitoring, with half of eligible patients willing to participate. Projects potential reductions in hospital admissions and consultations if remote monitoring is widely adopted across the EU.
market_sizing.source_title: How technology could cut millions of hospital visits across Europe

demand_drivers.driver: Broad applicability of AI in workflows
demand_drivers.description: Approximately 80% of life sciences workflows are deemed 'agentifiable', indicating widespread potential for AI integration to improve efficiency and productivity.

pnl_drivers.description: AI deployed at scale leads to a consistent 3% to 5% improvement in operating margins across life sciences companies, driven by efficiency gains and accelerated processes.

new_opportunities.description: About 40% of what AI agents can do represents work not currently undertaken due to prohibitive human time costs, opening new areas for value creation, such as reaching smaller customer segments or comprehensive compliance checks.

market_sizing.methodology: McKinsey's analysis across life sciences workflows, identifying 'agentifiable' tasks and observed impact of AI deployment at scale.
market_sizing.source_title: AI in life sciences explained: The technology that could reinvent medicine
